meaning: A program that holds a scene as numbers and computes how it moves, one small time step after another.
Training a policy from its own scored attempts; in simulation it consumes billions of physics steps.
The trained model that decides what the motors do next.
The full description of a simulated scene at one instant: every joint angle and joint speed, plus the position, orientation and motion of each loose object.
The amount of simulated time one physics step advances; 2 ms by default in MuJoCo and 5 ms in the SO-101 pick-cube task.
One call of the simulator's step function, which takes the state and the motor commands and returns the state one timestep later.
The text file of typed-in values that describes every link, joint, servo and shape of a scene.
One of the physics steps the simulator runs between two decisions of the policy; 20 in the SO-101 vision pick-cube task.
The time between two decisions of the policy; Playground rounds it to a whole number of timesteps.
A place where two simulated shapes touch, such as a finger on the cube.
The search, repeated every physics step, for which shapes in the scene touch, in a broad, a mid and a near phase.
The first, cheapest phase of collision detection, which picks out the pairs of bodies that could be touching.
A rule the next state must obey, for example that two touching shapes do not pass through each other.
Dry friction inside a joint, which MuJoCo models as a constraint; the SO-101 scene sets it on every joint.
The iterative search inside every physics step for the constraint forces that keep all constraints true at once.
The last part of a physics step, which uses accelerations to advance speeds and speeds to advance positions by one timestep.
The integration rule that updates the speed first and then moves the position with the new speed.
MuJoCo's recommended integrator, which rescales the acceleration using how speed-dependent forces such as damping change with speed.
A MuJoCo integrator its documentation recommends when stiff springs, position servos or strong damping interact with contacts.
A force that changes quickly with position or speed, which a large timestep applies wrongly and can make unstable.
The table that plays the role of mass for a jointed body, including how accelerating one joint loads the others.
The term c in the equation of motion: the pull of gravity and of the body's own motion.
A table with one row per constraint that says how far each joint's motion moves it; transposed, it turns constraint forces into joint forces.
MuJoCo's name for the vector of joint accelerations, the output of the force stages before integration.
MuJoCo's step function: 26 stages in four groups (position, velocity, force and acceleration, integrator).
One independent copy of the simulated scene with its own state; a GPU simulator advances thousands of them in one batch.
A world plus the task around it, the reward and the reset.
The maximum contacts and constraints each MuJoCo Warp world reserves up front (64 and 256 in the pick-cube task); memory and computation scale with them.
The time of one step, which CPU MuJoCo minimises, against the total steps per unit of time, which MuJoCo Warp maximises.
The part of the machine a job exhausts first; for CPU physics, the core itself.
Google DeepMind's open-source physics simulator, which steps one world on a CPU with low latency.
Google DeepMind's library of robot model files for MuJoCo, which includes the SO-101.
MuJoCo rewritten in NVIDIA's Warp framework to step many worlds in one batch on an NVIDIA GPU.
MuJoCo's JAX interface, over two engines: MJX-JAX, a rewrite in JAX, and MJX-Warp, which calls MuJoCo Warp.
Google's array library for Python, in which MJX-JAX is written.
Google DeepMind's suite of ready-made robot tasks and training code, which ships the SO-101 pick-cube task.
A GPU physics engine built on Warp that offers several solvers, MuJoCo Warp among them.
NVIDIA's physics engine, used by Isaac Sim and available to Isaac Lab.
NVIDIA's full simulator application, with PhysX physics and RTX rendering.
NVIDIA's robot-learning framework, which runs one task definition on Newton or PhysX and no longer needs Isaac Sim.
Running a simulator with no window and no camera images.
MuJoCo's timing tool: rolls a model out for 10,000 steps by default and prints CPU time, contact and constraint counts; --nthread runs one world per thread.
